summary: This informational document sets policy for including Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) in the definitive versions of RFCs and related publication formats. It keeps the policy requirements from RFC 7996 but drops requirements about a specific SVG profile or implementation code, and it obsoletes RFC 7996.

eli5.summary: RFCs can contain drawings. This sets the rules for the drawing file format used, so they show correctly everywhere.

subtitle: The policy for including SVG drawings in RFCs, leaving the tooling details to the RFC Production Center.

tldr.problem: RFC 7996 mixed policy about SVG drawings in RFCs with a specific SVG profile and implementation code.
tldr.mechanism: This document keeps the policy requirements, drops the profile and code requirements, and makes the RFC Production Center responsible for SVG tooling and implementation decisions.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7996. Drawings must not animate, script or link to external resources, and must not be the only way a concept is explained.

today: RFC 9896 obsoletes RFC 7996 and is an Informational document from the Editorial Stream. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines policy for including Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) in the definitive versions of RFCs and the publication formats defined in RFC 9720. SVG was developed by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C).

It takes the policy requirements from RFC 7996 but removes all requirements about using a specific SVG profile or implementation code. The RFC Production Center (RPC) decides on SVG tooling and implementation. It may use RFC 7996 as a starting point but is not bound by it.
sections.eli5: The rules say what drawings are allowed, and the publishing team chooses the exact tools.

sections.title: Policy Requirements
sections.content:
SVG drawings may help explain a concept, but they should not be its only representation. The text of the RFC should fully describe protocols, formats or architectures, and drawings should at minimum be consistent with it.

Drawings must not include animation or interactive features, and should include only limited reactive design elements such as scaling and dark/light mode. They must not contain pointers to external resources or executable script. They should be as accessible as possible, and the RPC refers to the W3C accessibility guidelines.

Authors may include multiple versions of an image in RFCXML, and each publication format should present the version best suited to it. SVG vocabulary and implementation may change over time, and changes need not stay backwards compatible, although compatibility is encouraged.
sections.eli5: A drawing can help, but the words must still explain everything. Drawings should not move, run programs, or fetch things from elsewhere.

sections.title: Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
The RPC may place technical and editorial constraints on SVG use, must document the acceptable usage, and must widely communicate changes to the RFC author community. It is expected to ask for community input before deciding and to explain its reasoning publicly.

Its implementation should try to allow drawings produced by widely used drawing tools, and should focus on specifying what is disallowed rather than exactly what is allowed. The RPC should periodically review its practices.
sections.eli5: The publishing team has to write down its rules, listen to authors, and say what is not allowed instead of listing every allowed thing.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The document states that it has no security considerations and no IANA actions. The ban on executable script and external resources in drawings is a policy requirement rather than a security section.
sections.eli5: There is nothing risky here to warn about, though the rules do keep drawings from running programs.

references.text: Brownlee, N., "SVG Drawings for RFCs: SVG 1.2 RFC", RFC 7996, December 2016.
Hoffman, P. and H. Flanagan, "RFC Formats and Versions", RFC 9720, January 2025.
